newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy appeals to Clinton about death-row man.
newsitem.headline: Italy appeals to Clinton about death-row man.

text.p: Italy said on Friday it had asked the United States to call off the execution of death-row prisoner Joseph O'Dell after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled to uphold the death sentence against him.
"The Italian government...is taking steps and has asked the U.S. authorities to suspend the execution of O'Dell," Patrizia Toia, a junior foreign minister, told reporters.
O'Dell was condemned to death in 1985 after being found guilty of killing a woman, but supporters say DNA testing proves he did not carry out the crime.

The state of Virginia had scheduled his execution for last December but the Court blocked the sentence at the last minute after a storm of protest, especially from Italy, where Pope John Paul and Prime Minister Romano Prodi led pleas for clemency.

Italy, which has no death penalty in civilian criminal cases, is among the most voiciferous advocates of a worldwide abolition of capital punishment. Italians staged street protests last December to call for a reprieve for O'Dell.
The Supreme Court on Thursday rejected the convicted murderer's claims that his death sentence should be overturned and said his execution could go ahead.
"We started to move on this as soon as we heard news that O'Dell's appeal had been rejected," Toia said.
Prodi, in Denver for a Group of Seven summit, told Italian reporters in Denver that he planned to raise the matter with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Toia said the initiative was in no way interference in the internal affairs of the U.S. but simply coherent with Italy's long-held stance against capital punishment.

"Three months after the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva approved a resolution presented by our government to abolish the death penalty, Italy finds itself in the face of a concrete case," Toia said.
"Far from interfering in U.S. affairs, the Italian initiative seeks to give a concrete and coherent follow-up to what was undertaken in Geneva," she said.
The Supreme Court ruling did not consider O'Dell's guilt or innocence, only whether he should receive the death penalty or should be re-sentenced to life in prison.

The court, by a 5-4 vote, rejected claims that the sentence should be overturned, although O'Dell can appeal to Virginia governor Allen. Allen had said he would wait for the ruling before deciding whether O'Dell should die by lethal injection.

Anti-death penalty group Hands off Cain staged a protest in front of the U.S. embassy in Rome on Friday together with human rights group Amnesty International. About 50 people took part including several politicians.
